title: The lamp that went out
told: from the verses of the first Buddhist nuns

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? has a pain ever lifted, and you only noticed once it was gone?
options: that quiet is what today is about. listen.
I’m in the middle of one
i’m so sorry. this story is for you most of all.

steps.line: Long ago, a woman named Patacara lost her whole family in one terrible stretch of days. Grief nearly broke her mind.
steps.label: as the old commentaries tell it

steps.line: She came to the Buddha with nothing left. “Sister,” he said gently, “come back to yourself.” She stayed, and became a nun.
steps.label: as the old commentaries tell it

steps.line: Years of practice passed. Still she wondered: farmers plough and their fields reward them. Why have I not found peace?
One evening, washing her feet, she watched the water run down the slope. She steadied her mind, the way you’d calm a good horse.

steps.q: The old commentary says she poured water three times: the first sank in soon, the next ran further, the third further still. What did she see in it?
o: Lives ending young, in middle age, or old
Her family, lost one after another
Each try at practice going a bit further
steps.why: The commentary on her verses says the water showed her how lives end early, midway or late. Her grief turned into insight into impermanence.

steps.q: That night she sits by her lamp and, with a needle, draws the wick down into the oil. What happens in her as the flame goes out?
o: She’s afraid of the dark again
steps.why: The flame goes out, and so does the last of her clinging. Her verse says her mind was set free.

steps.line: That night she sat by her lamp. With a needle, she drew down the wick.
The flame went out. “Like the lamp going out,” her verse says, “my mind was set free.”

steps.q: Nirvana is linked to a flame going out. What does the word itself literally mean?
steps.why: Nibbana (Sanskrit nirvana) means going out, like a fire, and also cooling. “Waking up” is bodhi, from the same root as the word Buddha.

steps.q: Patacara’s verses are kept in the Therigatha, the poems of the first Buddhist nuns. What makes it remarkable?
o: It was written by the Buddha himself
It’s among the oldest poems by women anywhere
It was kept secret from the monks
steps.why: Tradition says the early nuns composed these verses themselves, and they’ve been passed down for over two thousand years: one of the earliest collections of women’s poetry known.

steps.line: Today, at the end of a long day, a small quiet opens between two thoughts. The third truth points at moments like that.
steps.label: today

say: the buddha’s third truth is simple: the wobble can stop. when the thirst fades completely, dukkha ends. the word for that ending is nirvana, often linked to a flame going out.

not a heaven you travel to, and not blankness. an old verse calls it the highest happiness. a fire with nothing left to burn. buddhist traditions describe it in different words, and often say what it isn’t.

steps.q: Someone asks: when Patacara’s lamp went out, where did the flame go?
o: Up, to a realm of light
The question doesn’t fit. It just went out
Into the next flame that’s lit
steps.why: The Buddha once asked a wanderer: does a fire that has gone out go north, south, east or west? The question doesn’t fit. It had nothing left to burn.

today.say: tonight, before sleep, look for one small quiet: a moment when nothing is pulling at you, not a want, not an ache. it might be one breath long. that tiny gap is what the third truth points at.
options: tiny counts. that’s the flame, resting.
whenever you look, it will be there to find.

card.from: from the verses of the first Buddhist nuns
sources: Therigatha 5.10 (verses 112–116), Patacara: farmers ploughing and sowing; washing her feet and watching the water flow downhill; steadying the mind like a thoroughbred horse; taking a lamp into her cell, drawing the wick with a needle; “like the going out of the lamp was the liberation of my mind”
Dhammapada Commentary (on Dhammapada 113) and Therigatha Commentary: Patacara’s losses and the Buddha’s words “Sister, recover your presence of mind”
Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11): the third truth
Aggivacchagotta Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 72): which direction did the fire go
check: Her losses (husband, two sons, parents and brother) are compressed to “her whole family in one terrible stretch of days.”
“Come back to yourself” paraphrases “recover your presence of mind.”
Translations differ on whether she drew the wick down or pulled it out.
